1.pericope_label: Thus hath the Lord God shewed unto me: and behold a basket of summer fruit
debates: What the basket of summer fruit signifies
What passing by no more means
Why the prophet is questioned about what he sees
outliers: Calvin makes the ripeness belong to the punishment rather than to the people
Clarke reports a second view in which the fruit is the last of autumn, after which nothing more can be expected
themes: A song that sings sinners asleep
Fruit that will not keep till winter
Two Hebrew words a single letter apart
Correction withdrawn because it no longer corrects

3.pericope_label: And the songs of the temple shall be howlings in that day, saith the Lord God
debates: Whether the songs belong to a temple or a palace
How the clause about casting forth in silence is to be construed
Why the address is turned on the leaders
outliers: Clarke reports a conjecture that turns the songs into singing women who howl
Ellicott prefers a connected rendering over the abrupt ejaculations other commentators propose
themes: Prosperity read as a verdict of favour
Singing that answers a daily warning
Too few left alive to chant a dirge
Thirst for the ashes on a poor man head

5.pericope_label: Saying, When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat
debates: What the new moon here means
How the two frauds of measure and weight worked together
How the poor came to be bought at all
outliers: Gill reports readings that make the new moon the harvest month or the intercalated month rather than the monthly festival
Ellicott argues from the impatience itself that the festivals were kept in the northern kingdom though disliked
themes: Holy days wished away for market days
A symbol of justice made the instrument of fraud
Hoarded grain used to starve a people
Chaff sold to men who cannot sue

7.pericope_label: The Lord hath sworn by the excellency of Jacob, Surely I will never forget any of their works
debates: What the excellency of Jacob is that God swears by
Whether the trembling of the land is a literal earthquake
Why the threat is put as a question
outliers: Ellicott reconciles this oath with an earlier passage where the same excellency is abhorred
Calvin rejects an older rendering that made God swear against the pride of Jacob rather than by his dignity
themes: Men too hardened to be moved by reproof
A question asked where no doubt exists
Ground that cannot bear the people on it
A river that rises and then falls again

9.pericope_label: I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day
debates: Whether a real eclipse is referred to
What the darkening at noon stands for
Why feasts and songs are singled out for the reversal
outliers: Calvin flatly denies that any eclipse is meant and warns against literal reading of prophetic figures
Gill dates three eclipses to the three great feasts and lets the prophecy refer to them
themes: A figure argued over as an astronomical record
Light turned to darkness by the God who gave it
Ceremonies treated as dens for robbers
A bitter day following a dark night

11.pericope_label: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord God, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread
debates: When the famine of the word fell
Whether hungering for the word is itself a mercy
What territory the wandering covers
outliers: Calvin answers his own objection by denying that the hunger is sincere seeking, and compares the howling of Esau over a lost birthright
Ellicott reads the compass points as naming the very regions from which the people had sought divination
themes: A people that surfeited on preaching
Water in the well and nothing to draw with
Displeasure shown by silence
Agony that torments without repenting

13.pericope_label: In that day shall the fair virgins and young men faint for thirst
debates: Whether the thirst is figurative or literal
What the sin of Samaria is
What the manner of Beersheba means
outliers: Calvin breaks with the figure he has been following and reads this thirst as a real want of water
Ellicott turns the fainting of the young into a question about what becomes of them in later life
themes: The strongest chosen to show there is no escape
An idol named after the city that bred it
A word for way used to mean a whole religion
Worshippers crossing a frontier to pay vows
